Words that name a style, mood, speed, instrument, key, length or tempo outright are read as-is. Everything else goes to a description reader trained on 5,521 MusicCaps clips, each described by a musician and tagged with genre, mood and tempo. The tags were grouped into the page's 10 styles, 3 moods and 3 speeds. The reader averages the GloVe word vectors of your description and feeds the result to one logistic regression classifier per question (built in scikit-learn), with an extra learned weight for each word the musicians used. Because the classifiers are linear, the page can show which of your words drove each answer.

A recurrent neural network (a 2-layer GRU with 256 units, built in PyTorch) trained on 306 four-part Bach chorales from the music21 corpus, each moved to C major or A minor. It writes four parts on a grid of sixteenth notes, one cell at a time: the melody, the high harmony, the low harmony and the bass. At every cell it sees the token it just wrote, the note each part is holding, which part it is writing, where it is in the bar, major or minor, and how many bars are left, then picks the next token at random by its predicted chances. The Creativity slider sharpens or flattens those chances. Bright moods use a major key, and sad or dark moods use a minor key.

Each part stays inside the range Bach used for it, no part moves above the part written over it, two parts never move in parallel fifths or octaves, and the first note cannot be a hold. If the song does not end on the home chord, the model writes the last two bars again, up to 8 tries.

The style decides how each part is played: held, repeated on eighth notes like a rock guitar, broken into a harp arpeggio, played as jazz chord stabs over a walking bass, strummed, or played as oom-pah for a march. It also picks the drum beat, the usual band and a speed range. These patterns are fixed rules, not learned, and the drums are built from scratch in the browser with oscillators and noise.
Each spotlight follows its part's notes: it flares when a note starts, stays lit while the note rings, and fades when the part rests.

A note grid for writing music by hand, with no AI involved. It uses the same instruments, drums and player as the composer, can start from the AI's song, saves your work in your browser and exports MIDI.

The reader was scored on 20% of MusicCaps clips held out of training. The composer's next-note model was scored on 15% of the chorales held out of training (it guesses Bach's next new note exactly 58.0% of the time), and its songs were checked against the music theory rules in Test 2. The models on this page were then trained on all of the data.
Both models are compressed to 8-bit numbers and run in plain JavaScript, so nothing you type leaves your device.
